newsitem.title: ROMANIA: SOCCER-FREE MARKET FORCES SWEEP THROUGH ROMANIAN SOCCER.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-FREE MARKET FORCES SWEEP THROUGH ROMANIAN SOCCER.

text.p: Leading Romanian clubs Steaua and Dinamo are set to discard their old communist allegiances as free market reforms sweep through the country.

Following the centrists' triumph over the left-wingers in last November's election, Steaua is set to abandon its association with the army while Dinamo looks likely to split from the interior ministry.
Veteran trainer Emeric Ienei, recently appointed secretary of stage at the Sports Ministry, is behind the campaign to make the clubs independent of government departments.

"The top Romanian teams Steaua and Dinamo are already financially independent," Ienei said in an interview. "Both teams must discard the umbrella of the defence and the interior ministries respectively."
Ienei, 60, a former army colonel, was the trainer at Steaua in 1986 when they became the first east European team to win the European Cup.
"Departmental clubs are a late heritage of eastern Europe's old communist regiems," Ienei added. "It's time for them to leave the sports' stage."
After the fall of communism in 1989, Steaua and Dinamo amassed an estimated $25 million in transfer fees from the sale of dozens of leading players to western clubs.
But previous attempts to remove them from departmental control have been unsuccessful.
Dinamo declared its freedom from the Interior Ministry in 1992, only to have that decision over-ruled two years later by a local court.
Now club president Cornel Dinu believes Dinamo will thrive in a free market.
"Dinamo is already a professional club," he said.
Marcel Puscas, who took over as Steaua club president after reformists ousted leftists at last November's polls, has given a cautious welcome to Ienei's campaign.
"It's time for soccer teams to go independent," he said."But we shouldn't jump overboard without thinking twice in order to find the right way to reach that aim."
Ienei also believes first division sides Rapid and Sportul Studentesc should fully abandon state subsidies.

"It's not normal that Rapid's sponsoring should be shared by a private businessman and the Transport Ministry or that Sportul Studentesc should have the Education Ministry as their main boss," he said.
Despite his commitment to reforms, Ienei, who is effectively Romania's Sports Minister, believes state subsidies are still necessary in other sport.
"Gymnastics, canoeing, rowing, handball, weightlifting and others, also the glory of Romanian sports, cannot survive without state finance in our emerging market economy," he said,
